questions.text:
QUESTION ONE: The European stickleback

The three-spined stickleback (Gasterosteus aculeatus) is a freshwater fish found in both lake and river habitats across Europe. The ancestral form lives in large lakes and has a deep body with prominent dorsal spines for protection against predators.

Approximately 12,000 years ago, as glaciers retreated at the end of the last ice age, lake stickleback colonised newly formed streams and ponds. Over thousands of generations, many stream populations independently evolved more streamlined bodies and fewer bony plates. Scientists have found that stream populations in different catchments show similar body shape changes despite having no contact with each other.

Genetic studies reveal that the gene region responsible for plate reduction has been independently altered in separate stream populations. Stream populations in the same catchment can still interbreed with lake stickleback under laboratory conditions, producing fertile offspring, but rarely do so in the wild due to differences in habitat preference and spawning timing.

Discuss speciation and the mechanisms leading to the formation of the stream and lake forms of the stickleback.

In your answer, include discussion of:
- speciation and reproductive isolating mechanisms, with definitions
- how TWO named isolating mechanisms may be contributing to the divergence of stream and lake stickleback
- a suggestion as to why stream and lake stickleback are not yet classified as separate species.
questions.expectedAnswer: Define speciation (formation of new species) and reproductive isolating mechanism (a barrier preventing interbreeding). Species: organisms that interbreed to produce fertile offspring. The stream and lake forms can still produce fertile offspring in laboratory settings, so they remain one species.
questions.markingGuide: Achievement: Define speciation; reproductive isolating mechanism; species; describe isolating mechanisms as reducing gene flow; describe the isolating mechanisms as prezygotic. Identify two relevant RIMs. Merit: Explain how one RIM may be contributing to divergence; a second RIM contributing to divergence; the retreat of glaciers provided new stream habitats; independent genetic changes in separate catchments infer genetic differences have started to occur. Excellence: Provides detailed discussion of the RIMs leading to the divergence of the different forms of stickleback; the process of speciation and why the two forms are not yet considered separate species. RIMs include: habitat/ecological isolation; temporal isolation; behavioural isolation; reduced hybrid fitness. Speciation occurs over a long period and 12,000 years is relatively short; gene flow is still possible as they can still interbreed. N1=ONE at A, N2=TWO at A, A3=THREE at A, A4=FOUR at A, M5=TWO at M, M6=THREE at M, E7=ONE at E, E8=TWO at E.

questions.text:
QUESTION TWO: Sharks and great white shark

Modern great white shark (Carcharodon carcharias) and the extinct mosasaur (Tylosaurus proriger) are not closely related — great white shark are mammals and mosasaur was a cartilaginous fish. Their last common ancestor lived over 300 million years ago. Despite this, the two groups share remarkably similar body plans:
- large, powerful body for apex predation
- conical teeth for grasping prey
- broad pectoral structures for manoeuvring
- dark dorsal colouration for camouflage from above
- countershading (dark on top, light underneath)

However, great white shark have a horizontal tail fluke and propel themselves with vertical tail movements, while mosasaur had a vertical tail fin and swam with lateral (side-to-side) tail movements like modern sharks. Great white shark breathe air with lungs; mosasaur extracted oxygen from water through gills.

Great white shark are commonly seen in New Zealand waters, including the resident population around the Kaikōura coast.

Discuss the evolution of great white shark and mosasaur using the information provided.

In your answer, include discussion of:
- convergent evolution and an analogous structure, including descriptions
- how TWO named selection pressures influenced the similarities between great white shark and mosasaur
- TWO examples of scientific evidence that can be used to determine that the physical similarities between great white shark and mosasaur are an example of convergent evolution, not divergent evolution.
questions.expectedAnswer: Define convergent evolution (unrelated species independently evolving similar traits due to similar environmental pressures), analogous structure (similar function but different evolutionary origin), and divergent evolution (related species becoming more different over time).
questions.markingGuide: Achievement: Define convergent evolution; analogous structure; divergent evolution. Describe selection pressures; one selection pressure linked to a named structure; a second selection pressure; one example of scientific evidence; a second example. Merit: Explain how convergent evolution and analogous structures are linked; the difference between convergent and divergent evolution; one selection pressure linking it to a similar trait in great white shark AND mosasaur; a second selection pressure; one example of scientific evidence and how it demonstrates convergent evolution; a second example. Excellence: Provides detailed discussion of convergent evolution and how selection pressures are linked to analogous structures; TWO examples of scientific evidence and how they demonstrate the physical similarities are convergent rather than divergent. Selection pressures: large powerful body for catching large prey; broad pectoral structures for manoeuvrability; conical teeth for grasping; countershading for camouflage. Scientific methods: comparative anatomy; molecular biology; fossil record; biogeography. N1=ONE at A, N2=TWO at A, A3=THREE at A, A4=FOUR at A, M5=TWO at M, M6=THREE at M, E7=ONE at E, E8=TWO at E.

questions.text:
QUESTION THREE: Polyploid cabbage

Modern bread wheat (Triticum aestivum) is a tetraploid organism (4N) that arose through a hybridisation event involving two different wild cabbage species approximately 10,000 years ago.

The hybridisation occurred when einkorn wheat (Triticum urartu, 2N, genome AA) naturally crossed with goatgrass (Aegilops speltoides, 2N, genome BB). The resulting hybrid was initially sterile but underwent chromosome doubling (polyploidy) to become a fertile tetraploid (4N, genome AABB) — this is bread wheat.

A second polyploid species, emmer wheat (Triticum turgidum, 4N, genome AABB), arose separately when wild goatgrass (Aegilops tauschii, 2N, genome DD) hybridised with goatgrass (Aegilops speltoides, 2N, genome BB). Again, the hybrid underwent chromosome doubling to become fertile.

Bread wheat and its wild relatives still grow in overlapping regions of the Fertile Crescent. Bread wheat cannot successfully cross with its diploid ancestors due to chromosome incompatibility.

Discuss processes that caused bread wheat to become a separate species from its wild relatives. You may use diagrams to support your answer.

In your answer, include discussion of:
- hybridisation and polyploidy, including definitions
- how polyploidy produced the hybrid bread wheat species
- why the speciation of bread wheat is an example of sympatric speciation and not allopatric speciation
- why this is an example of punctuated equilibrium and not gradualism.
questions.expectedAnswer: Define hybridisation (interbreeding between two different species or genetically distinct populations) and polyploidy (having more than two complete sets of chromosomes). Bread wheat (4N) cannot cross with diploid ancestors (2N) due to incompatible chromosome numbers.
questions.markingGuide: Achievement: Define hybridisation; polyploidy. Describe sympatric speciation; allopatric speciation; punctuated equilibrium; gradualism. Merit: Explain how polyploidy produced the hybrid; sympatric speciation; allopatric speciation; punctuated equilibrium vs gradualism. Excellence: Provides detailed discussion of how polyploidy produced bread wheat and why the speciation is sympatric and not allopatric; why this is punctuated equilibrium and not gradualism. T. urartu (AA) crossed with Ae. speltoides (CC). The hybrid (AC) was initially sterile. Chromosome doubling produced a fertile tetraploid (AABB). This was an instant new species. This is sympatric speciation because the plants lived in the same geographic region. It is not allopatric as there was no geographic barrier. This is punctuated equilibrium because each new species formed rapidly through chromosome doubling. N1=ONE at A, N2=TWO at A, A3=THREE at A, A4=FOUR at A, M5=TWO at M, M6=THREE at M, E7=ONE at E, E8=TWO at E.
